yaml.title: Welcome to my blog
yaml.description: A first post — what this space is for and what you can expect to find here.

markdown.markdown:
This is the first post on my blog, so it seems worth saying a few words
about what this space is for.

I study mathematics. Most of what that means, day to day, is reading —
working through proofs, getting stuck, going back, understanding something
a little better than you did before. It's a slow and private process, and
there's not much obvious output to show for it while it's happening.

This blog is partly an attempt to make that process a little more visible,
and partly a way of forcing myself to write. There is a certain kind of
understanding you only arrive at when you try to explain something to
someone else — I'm hoping this is useful for that.


A few things I have in mind:

- **Expository notes** on mathematics I'm learning — definitions, theorems,
  examples, and the kind of context that textbooks sometimes skip.
- **Problems I find interesting** — not necessarily hard ones, just ones
  where the solution surprised me or where I think the journey is worth
  documenting.
- **Reflections on studying** — what's working, what isn't, and things I
  wish someone had told me earlier.

I'll also write about [any other topics you'd like — tutoring, books, etc.].

## A small example

To set the tone, here is a fact I find genuinely delightful. The sum of
the first $n$ odd numbers is always a perfect square:

$$
1 + 3 + 5 + \cdots + (2n - 1) = n^2
$$

You can see why this is true without any algebra at all — just draw it:

```
■           (n = 1, sum = 1)
■ □
□ □         (n = 2, sum = 4)
■ □ □
□ □ □
□ □ □       (n = 3, sum = 9)
```

Each new odd number adds an L-shaped border to the previous square, and
the result is always a square. That's a proof — and a beautiful one.

This is the kind of thing I hope to write more of.
